title: 'Bad language, threats': WA politicians have had enough of copping it online

Topic:State and Territory Government

One Nation MP-elect Luke Herdegen was subject to media scrutiny — both online and IRL — this week. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The political arena has never been for the faint of heart, but social media has taken what elected officials have to contend with to a whole other level.

It's an issue Labor, the Liberals and One Nation have grappled with this week, each in their own way.

Western Australia's Liberal MP Andrew Hastie declared war on One Nation over an online cartoon that dubbed the former Special Air Service (SAS) officer a "traitor" for giving evidence in a defamation case against SAS veteran Ben Roberts-Smith.

And long-serving WA Labor minister Simone McGurk also highlighted the perils of social media when she shared some of the "bad language, threats of violence, and questionable grammar" she cops on her feeds.

WA Labor MP McGurk says those perpetrating online abuse must be called out. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Once women got there [sic] foot into parliament were [sic] stuffed," one comment read.

"F**k I'd love to push that skank out the window," another person had written.

Ms McGurk, who has been in parliament since 2013, said it was "incredible" to see how negative some comments could be.

"And often we find that it's not actually bots … it is actually real people who are deciding to put pretty vulgar, abusive content and feedback online," she told reporters on Friday.

That's what Hastie did this week when he fired up over the cartoon posted by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson on her X account in July.

He first put the orange team in his sights on Tuesday, declaring he would "never back down" from a fight with Labor and One Nation after Hanson said he would not be spared in her pursuit of WA seats at the next federal election.

Liberal MP Hastie has locked horns with One Nation's Pauline Hanson over the cartoon. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Hastie then spent the next two days declaring she had "picked a fight with the wrong veteran".

"There are thousands, if not millions, of Australians around this country who would take offence at the use of the word 'traitor'," he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Hanson has refused to delete the video, but her WA lieutenant had a different view.

"I'm not going to condone calling anyone a traitor that served our country," WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies told reporters on Thursday.

One Nation WA leader Caddies says he rarely speaks to Senator Hanson. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I'd prefer every party, including our own party, have the temperature down."

Not that he's planning to tell Hanson that anytime soon, saying: "I hardly speak to Pauline."

Caddies argued that a protest which took criticism of his MP-elect that he had minimised domestic violence offline and onto the steps of Parliament didn't meet that standard.

"This protest was kind of couched in the absurd and the theatrical, but it's so important that we have these conversations in all these different mediums," Greens MP Jess Beckerling said.

Luke Herdegen had told the ABC's 7.30 "it's not something that anyone is talking about in the community here", when asked about Hanson's comments that domestic violence is a two-way street.

"What I was referring to was that people weren't talking about Pauline's comments," Herdegen said on Tuesday.

"I believe that all people should be protected from domestic violence … It certainly happens to both males and females."

The protesters wanted Herdegen to work out with them in front of the WA Parliament. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

It prompted a unique protest, with attendees encouraging the gym owner to work out with them in front of state parliament.

Herdegen watched on but didn't participate.

One Nation also wasn't impressed with the standards of "The Gherk", an AI-generated pickle that threw shade on the party's MP-elect, Luke Herdegen this week before acknowledging it had got it wrong.

In a post to its 71,000 Facebook followers, the page claimed to have been contacted by someone involved in getting Herdegen into his new office who said he "isn't answering" calls.

Satirical page 'The Gherk' has more than 70,000 followers on Facebook. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Herdegen was quick to respond, saying he had met with the "handover team" the week before and plans were in place.

The state government, which manages electorate offices, was also confused, saying it had "only contacted the new member" and "there have been no delays to this process".

Herdegen took to Facebook too to defend himself from The Gherk. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

In response to questions from the ABC, "The Gherk" said they had no "independent way of verifying" their contact's employment, only that they said they were "not an employee of the state" as of the day before the election, and that they "spoke in detail about the handover".

Social media is a messy and ever-evolving part of the political landscape.

The head of Instagram says the average person who turns off their algorithm will have a much worse "user experience", as Australia debates new opt-out laws.

While it provides a new way for representatives to connect with the represented, there are plenty of signs it's not as simple as that.

That's without even getting into the issue of bots and AI — a problem raised repeatedly by Labor during and after the Secret Harbour campaign, and which Premier Roger Cook said this week drove an online debate over migration driven by "hatred".

Contact Keane Bourke on encrypted email.

Please note you will need your own encrypted email account, such as Protonmail, to ensure end-to-end encryption.

Premier Roger Cook wants more oversight online. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I remember the day that television got introduced into our house, and in those days we were all anxious about the impact that television would have on our society," Cook said on Tuesday.

"My parents used to limit us to 30 minutes of television a day, which meant you could either watch Gilligan's Island or Brady Bunch, you couldn't watch both.

The federal Labor government's attempts to better regulate social media try to do just that.

But in an increasingly contested political landscape, social media might just be a symptom of much deeper divides.
